title: Plain wood, soon
hookLine: burial comes quickly, often in a plain wooden coffin

lines: A PINE BOX IN THE CORNER.
cards: A showroom at a funeral home. Polished mahogany with brass rails, a quilted satin lining, a model with a name like a luxury car. And in the corner, almost apologetic, a simple box of unfinished pine.

A family sits down with a salesman, still in shock, the phone buzzing with relatives booking flights. For Jewish families who keep the tradition, two decisions are made before they walk in. The box will be the plain one.
And the funeral will be soon.

teach.h: NO ONE SPENDS TO SHOW LOVE.
teach.b: The plain coffin follows from yesterday: everyone equal in death, and no family made to feel it has to spend to show love.
Traditional coffins are simple wood, unpolished, and some are made without metal at all, joined with wooden pegs. Then the earth.
After Eden, God tells Adam, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." A plain wooden box lets that happen.
It doesn't try to hold back the earth; it lets the body go home. In some places, Jews are buried in shrouds alone, with no coffin at all. Then the clock.

The Torah, speaking about someone executed and hung up, says the body must not stay up overnight but be buried that same day. The rabbis drew a wider principle: leaving the dead unburied is a disgrace, so bury promptly.
That's why a Jewish funeral can come so fast, sometimes within a day. And the exception.
Waiting can serve the dead person's honor too. The Talmud allows a delay for the sake of the dead, to bring a coffin or shrouds, and later codes add time for close relatives to arrive.
What isn't allowed is delay for its own sake. The rule and the exception point the same way: what honors this person? Both are about the person in the box, not the people looking at it.

how: Traditional Jewish burial takes place soon after death, with short delays allowed for the honor of the deceased, such as for close relatives to arrive; the coffin is usually plain unfinished wood, and in some places the body is buried in shrouds without a coffin.

o: a simple coffin, the same for all, and a quick burial
a polished coffin that shows the family's love
a carved box kept at home to hold a loved one's things

s: Jewish law forbids any delay in burial
a delay is allowed for the dead person's honor: the Talmud names a coffin or shrouds, and later codes add close relatives arriving.
some traditional coffins are made without metal
some are joined with wooden pegs, so the body can return to the earth.
a finer coffin honors the dead more

games.q: your father has died. your sister is on a flight from overseas and lands tomorrow night. what does the tradition allow?
o: bury today; no one can wait.
a short delay so close relatives can arrive, for his honor.
wait a few weeks so everyone can plan.
games.why: Jewish law allows a delay for the sake of the dead, and the codes count close relatives arriving; delay for its own sake is not the point.

practice: Find one plain thing near you made of wood, cloth or stone, a table, a chair, a doorframe, and rest your eyes or your hand on it.
Notice how it asks for no attention and still does its job every day, then ask where, in your own life, plain would do. If you pray, you can hold the line about dust in your mind, or sit in silence.

wordCard.voice: Plain wood. A simple coffin, the same for everyone, letting the body return to the earth, and a burial that comes soon, for the honor of the dead. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a box or chest; the word used for a coffin.

carryVoice: Your line: plain wood. Simple honors the dead better than show. Back tomorrow, same hill.
